Nakshaa Retail Systems: Forty-One Seconds a Shop

A Pune software company sells the number by which two lakh Indian salesmen are judged, and is paid a bonus when that number goes up. It has gone up for nine quarters. On Saturday the chief product officer spent eleven hours in a distributor's van in Solapur, and he now has to decide, by Monday, whether the number means anything at all — and whether he is allowed to change it.

1. Sunday night, Baner

At 10.40 p.m. on Sunday, 12 April 2026, Siddharth Apte sat at the dining table of his flat in Baner, Pune, with a printout of a single day's visit log and a cup of tea he had forgotten twice. The log belonged to a salesman named Ganesh Pawar, who worked for a distributor in Solapur, and whom Siddharth had accompanied for eleven hours the previous day in the back of a Bolero that smelled of biscuit cartons.

The log said that Pawar had made 39 productive calls. Siddharth had counted the shops with his own eyes: they had entered 22. In 14 of the remaining 17, Pawar had stopped the van at the kerb, opened the Nakshaa app, marked the visit, marked "no order – stock sufficient", and driven on. He had not been hiding it. At the eighth such stop he had handed Siddharth the phone so that he could see the green tick, and said, in Marathi, that the beat plan for that day had 44 shops in it, that 44 was not possible in Solapur in April, that his incentive required 82 per cent productive calls, and that everybody — his supervisor, the distributor, the regional manager — knew this and had known it for two years.

Nakshaa Retail Systems computed that 82 per cent. It published it, benchmarked it, put it on a leaderboard, and — under a clause its founders had signed in August 2023 — was paid ₹1.15 crore a year, or not paid it, depending on whether it stayed above that line at its largest customer.

The product steering committee met at 9.30 a.m. on Monday in the Baner office, with the board's two independent directors attending as observers. Item two was Siddharth's paper, "Visit Integrity: options". It had four options in it. Sitting at his dining table with Pawar's log in front of him, Siddharth was no longer certain that any of the four was about the thing that was actually wrong.

2. How Nakshaa got here

Nakshaa Retail Systems was founded in Pune in 2019 by Vaishali Kamat, who had spent eleven years in sales operations at a packaged-foods company, and Harish Iyer, an engineer who had built offline-first Android applications for a rural banking correspondent network. Their insight was unglamorous and correct: India's general trade is served by roughly a crore of small shops, visited on foot and on two-wheelers by field salesmen following a weekly "beat" plan, and almost none of that work was instrumented. Nakshaa's application let a salesman record a visit, take an order, check stock and claim a scheme, working offline and syncing when a signal returned.

By April 2026 Nakshaa had 214 customers, 1.42 lakh paid rep seats, revenue of about ₹38 crore, and 240 employees, most of them in Pune and Bengaluru. It competed with established Indian field-force platforms and with the in-house systems of the largest consumer companies, and it was visibly the smallest of the credible players.

In 2021 the company shipped the feature that made its name. The Nakshaa Score was a composite of six inputs — visit compliance, productive call rate, lines per call, new outlets added, scheme compliance and range sold — expressed out of 100 and refreshed daily. It was designed as a coaching tool for supervisors. Within a year customers had wired it into rep incentives, and by 2023 two customers were using it in performance-improvement processes. Nobody at Nakshaa had designed it for that, and nobody at Nakshaa had objected.

The decision that constrains everything about the present situation was taken in August 2023. To win Shubhankar Consumer Products — an Ahmedabad packaged-foods company with 2,900 field reps, then the largest deal in Nakshaa's history at ₹6.4 crore a year — Vaishali agreed to a performance-linked commercial. Eighteen per cent of the annual fee, ₹1.15 crore, sits at risk against two thresholds: a productive call rate of 82 per cent and visit compliance of 90 per cent, both computed by Nakshaa's own software from data captured by Nakshaa's own application. The contract also contains, at Shubhankar's insistence and drafted by their legal team, a methodology clause: the definitions underlying the Nakshaa Score and its component metrics may not be materially changed during the term without Shubhankar's prior written consent, so that year-on-year comparisons in their internal reporting remain valid.

Siddharth, who joined in 2024, has read that clause eleven times. It means that the company cannot fix its own measurement without the written permission of the customer whose reps have the strongest reason to refuse.

3. The industry

The economics of Indian general trade are shifting under everyone in this market. Quick commerce — Zepto, Blinkit, Swiggy Instamart — has taken a visible share of urban impulse and top-up purchases, and the large consumer companies have responded by demanding more, not less, from their general-trade coverage: more outlets billed, wider range per outlet, faster response to competitive activity. ONDC has made small-shop digital ordering cheaper to attempt. GST e-invoicing has made secondary sales data cleaner at the distributor level than it was five years ago, which matters here, because it means a customer can now check a claim that it once could not.

Field-force software in India sells at ₹180 to ₹260 per rep per month, a price that has not moved in five years, against Gulf and South-East Asian markets where the same product sells at two to three times that. Nakshaa's foreign revenue is therefore small in seats and material in margin. Its anchor international customer is Kanz Distribution, a Dubai group distributing fourteen brands across the UAE and Oman with 640 reps, worth ₹4.9 crore a year, and Kanz's chief operating officer has asked to extend the Nakshaa Score into rep incentives across both countries.

Two regulatory facts bear directly on Monday's decision. The first is the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, under which continuous location processing of employees requires a lawful basis, notice and a grievance mechanism; Nakshaa's counsel has advised that using location data to generate inferences about an individual rep's honesty is a materially different processing purpose from operational visit logging, and has recommended that any such inference not be surfaced to the customer at rep level without fresh notice. The second is the ordinary commercial fact that nine of Nakshaa's ten largest contracts contain some form of productivity commitment, because that is how the company learned to sell.

4. The situation in detail

The timeline that matters begins with a usability complaint. In February 2024, after the Shubhankar rollout, the largest category of support tickets was reps unable to mark visits in areas with poor connectivity or GPS drift — dense bazaars in old Pune and Ahmedabad, basement shops, rural Maharashtra in the afternoon. Harish Iyer's team shipped offline visit capture in April 2024. Its rules, which were written into a Jira ticket and never into a policy document, were three: the GPS tolerance for matching a visit to an outlet widened from 50 metres to 250 metres; a visit captured offline and synced later was accepted on the basis of the outlet code and a timestamp within the beat window, without any location check; and a visit with a captured "reason for no order" counted as productive.

Everybody in the company believed, in April 2024, that this was a fix for a connectivity problem. It was also, and was not seen to be, a complete description of how to record a shop you have not entered.

Through 2024 and 2025 every number the company watched improved. Verified visits processed — Nakshaa's own internal headline metric, reported to the board monthly — rose from 2.4 crore a month to 4.1 crore. Average productive call rate across the customer base rose from 71 to 84 per cent. At Shubhankar it rose from 74 to 86, and the at-risk fee was earned in eight consecutive quarters. Brian Kessler's team in New Jersey began selling on the strength of it: the pitch deck for the North American market carries a slide headed "Guaranteed productivity uplift", with a median of eleven points.

In November 2025 a distributor in Nagpur wrote to Shubhankar's regional office, in a letter about a discount dispute, a paragraph that has since travelled a long way. He said that the system was showing 31 shops visited in his territory on days when his own two salesmen had been at a wedding, and that he had raised it with the area sales manager, who had told him it was not his concern.

Shubhankar's commercial team asked Nakshaa for an explanation. Wei Ling Tan's customer-success group in Singapore ran the standard diagnostic, found the offline share of visits in that territory to be 44 per cent against a national average of 19, attributed it to network coverage, and closed the ticket. In January 2026 Ritika Sen, in Toronto, went further and built the analysis that is now Exhibit 4. She did not set out to find fraud; she had been asked to improve the Score's predictive power against secondary sales, which had been deteriorating for a year without anyone treating it as a symptom.

What has since turned out to be wrong is not one thing but three. Offline capture is used most heavily not where the network is weakest but where beat plans are largest. The Score's correlation with the outcome it was meant to proxy — shops actually served — has fallen from 0.61 to 0.24 over two years, on Ritika's numbers. And the customer did not notice, because the customer's own managers are measured on the same number.

5. The people

Vaishali Kamat, 45, co-founder and chief executive, Pune. Position: the Nakshaa Score is the company's only real brand asset and cannot be disowned in public. She favours adding new measures beside it and changing nothing about the Score itself before the Shubhankar renewal. Incentive: she negotiated the August 2023 clause personally, and a Series B extension is in early conversations at a valuation anchored on 40 per cent growth. What she is not saying: she has begun to believe the performance-linked structure was a mistake, and she has not said this to Brian Kessler, whose entire North American pipeline is built on it.

Siddharth Apte, 39, chief product officer, Pune, the protagonist. Position: has not settled one. Incentive: he owns the roadmap and the Score, joined after the contract was signed, and has the standing of someone who can say the previous regime was wrong — once. What he is not saying: he has not told Vaishali that he rode with a rep on Saturday, or that the rep showed him the gaming without embarrassment.

Harish Iyer, 43, co-founder and vice-president of engineering, Bengaluru. Position: tightening verification will break the product for the reps who need it most, and he can cite three years of tickets. He proposes a hardware-assisted approach — Bluetooth beacons at outlets — costing ₹340 per outlet, which for Shubhankar's 4.1 lakh outlets is ₹13.9 crore that nobody will pay. Incentive: he wrote the 250-metre tolerance. What he is not saying: he knew within a month of shipping that offline share was rising fastest in high-beat-count territories, and he logged it as a performance note, not a risk.

Ritika Sen, 34, senior data scientist, Toronto. Position: the Score should be suspended as an incentive input until it can be validated against billed outlets. Incentive: her analysis is the strongest work she has done and she would like it acted on. What she is not saying: her gaming-signature model has never been validated against ground truth beyond 19 field audits, and its flags correlate with territory connectivity almost as strongly as with beat size, which means it may be labelling poor infrastructure as dishonesty.

Annika Brandt, 36, head of design, Berlin. Position: the product is adversarial and the gaming is a rational response to an impossible instruction; the design problem is the beat plan, not the verification. Incentive: she has been asking for a rep-side research budget for four quarters. What she is not saying: her own last round of research covered 14 reps, all urban, and the impossibility claim in Exhibit 6 rests on a sample she would not accept from anyone else.

Wei Ling Tan, 41, director of customer success, Singapore, covering South-East Asia and the Gulf. Position: whatever is decided must not be described to customers as a defect in past reporting. Incentive: her team's quarterly bonus is tied to renewals and to customer scores staying above contracted thresholds; she personally closed the Nagpur ticket. What she is not saying: two other customers have asked variations of the Nagpur question in the last five months and she has handled both without escalating.

Brian Kessler, 50, senior vice-president of sales, New Jersey. Position: keep the Score, keep the guarantee, and delay any announcement until after the Kanz signature. Incentive: his commission plan pays on new annual contract value and his largest open deal, a US consumer-products company, has asked for the same performance-linked structure. What he is not saying: he has already shared the "guaranteed productivity uplift" slide with that prospect's procurement team.

Ayesha Rahman, 38, chief operating officer, Kanz Distribution, Dubai. Position: wants the Score wired into rep incentives across the UAE and Oman from July, and has said so in writing. Incentive: her own board has approved a productivity programme that assumes it. What she is not saying: her reps are on employment visas tied to the employer, which makes an incentive metric a far heavier instrument in Dubai than in Solapur, and she has not raised this with anyone at Nakshaa.

7. Voices

"Saheb, if I enter all 44 shops properly I finish at nine at night and I still miss six. If I miss six my incentive is gone. The company wants 44, the phone wants a green tick. I give both of them what they want and I go home at seven. Tell me which part of this you want me to stop."

Ganesh Pawar, field salesman, Solapur, to Siddharth Apte, 11 April 2026

"We cannot be the company that tells its largest customer that the number in its own quarterly review has been wrong for two years, three weeks before the renewal notice. I am not saying we do nothing. I am saying we do not say that."

Vaishali Kamat, leadership call, 7 April 2026

"Twenty-three per cent is not a finding, it is a headline. My flag rate in the worst-connectivity decile is 36 per cent and in the largest-beat decile it is 43, and those two deciles share 60 per cent of their territories. If this goes to a customer at rep level, somebody in Nagpur loses a job over my threshold choice. I will not put my name on that."

Ritika Sen, analytics review, Toronto, 9 April 2026, 11.00 EDT (8.30 p.m. IST)

"We did not build a coaching tool that got misused. We built a scoreboard, sold it as a scoreboard, priced it as a scoreboard, and then acted surprised that people play to the scoreboard. Every one of our six inputs can be improved without a single extra shop being served. I have a list. It is one page."

Annika Brandt, product review, Berlin, 8 April 2026

"Please confirm by the 15th that the Score will be available for incentive computation from July. Our HR committee has approved the programme on that basis and the employment contracts for the new intake reference it."

"For the record, I closed the Nagpur ticket because the diagnostic said high offline share and the playbook says that is a coverage issue. The playbook is ours. If the playbook was wrong, please do not let Monday's minutes say that Singapore missed it."

Wei Ling Tan, message to Siddharth Apte, 11 April 2026

8. The options as Siddharth currently sees them

Option 1: ship Visit Integrity v2 across the base. Tolerance to 80 metres, a location fix required within four hours of any offline sync, and a distinct visual state for unverified visits. On the pilot's evidence this costs about nine points of productive call rate and nothing in orders. It also breaches the 82 per cent threshold at Shubhankar within a quarter, puts ₹1.15 crore at risk, and — on counsel's reading — is a material change to the methodology requiring Shubhankar's written consent, which means asking a customer whose managers are measured on the number to approve a change that will lower it.

Option 2: leave the Score alone and publish a second number beside it. An outcome index built from unique outlets billed, orders per recorded visit and retailer callback confirmation — measures that fall when visits are fabricated and that no rep can move from the kerb. Nothing breaks, nothing has to be confessed, and the contract is untouched. Against it: the incentive money still sits on the old number, the new index is reported monthly against a daily leaderboard, and Nakshaa has no way to compute retailer confirmation at scale without paying for outbound calls at about ₹14 a shop.

Option 3: get out of the scoring business. Keep the raw measures, withdraw the composite Score and the leaderboard, and reposition the product as a coverage and ordering system whose customers build their own incentive logic. This ends the company's exposure to how the number is used. It also removes the differentiator the New Jersey pitch is built on, invites the question of what Nakshaa has been selling since 2021, and does nothing at all about the fabricated visits, which are a problem of verification, not of composition.

Option 4: disclose to Shubhankar first, decide afterwards. Take Exhibits 4 and 6 to their commercial team before the 30 April notice date, ask for consent to change methodology, and propose a joint review of beat sizes. This is the only option that treats the customer as an adult. It also hands a renewal negotiation a quantified claim that Nakshaa has been paid a bonus on an inflated number for eight quarters, and Ritika will not certify the 23 per cent, and counsel has flagged that rep-level inference disclosure raises DPDP questions that have not been worked through.

On the back of the last page Siddharth has written two lines he has shown to nobody. The first is that all four options treat the fabricated visit as the defect, when the pilot suggests that the visits removed by verification were producing nothing, and Exhibit 6 suggests the beat plan asks for sixty per cent more than a day contains. The second is a question: if a rep is instructed to do forty-four impossible things and the software records him doing them, which of the two is the product — and whether a company whose entire commercial model is being paid when a number goes up can be trusted to answer that. He does not know how to put either line on a slide.

9. The deadline and the hard constraints

The product steering committee meets at 9.30 a.m. IST on Monday, 13 April 2026. Shubhankar's renewal notice is due by 30 April; the account is 17 per cent of revenue and its reference value is larger than that. The Kanz expansion, ₹3.1 crore, requires a written confirmation by 15 May that the Score will be available for incentive computation from July, and Ayesha Rahman's new-intake employment contracts already reference it. Nakshaa's cash is ₹26 crore against a net burn of ₹1.6 crore a month; a Series B extension is in early conversation at a valuation anchored on 40 per cent growth, and Q4 growth was 31 per cent. The methodology clause binds until the Shubhankar term ends in March 2027. Engineering capacity for the June quarter is 19 developer-months, of which 7 are committed to GST e-invoice reconciliation that three customers have made a condition of renewal; Visit Integrity v2 is estimated at 6, and Harish's beacon proposal at 11 plus ₹13.9 crore of hardware nobody has budgeted. Retailer callback confirmation at base scale would cost about ₹1.9 crore a year. Counsel has advised that surfacing rep-level authenticity inferences to customers requires fresh notice and a grievance mechanism under the DPDP Act, which is four to six weeks of work not currently scheduled. Brian Kessler's commission plan for FY27 has been communicated and pays on new annual contract value. Ritika Sen has said, in writing, that she will not certify the 23 per cent figure for external use.

10. Questions for discussion

1. List the six inputs of the Nakshaa Score and, for each, name the cheapest way a rep could improve it without serving one additional shop. Which of the six is hardest to move that way, and why was it not weighted more heavily in 2021?

2. Exhibit 2 and Exhibit 3 describe the same salesmen over the same period and point in opposite directions. Which is measuring what the company sells, and which is measuring what the customer buys? What single measure, had it been on the board pack in 2024, would have caught the divergence first — and who would have had to own it?

3. Exhibit 4 flags 23 per cent of visits and Exhibit 6 removes 21 per cent of them at a cost of 2 per cent of orders. State precisely what each exhibit can and cannot support. What would you need to add to Exhibit 4 before you would put a rep's name next to a flag, and what would it cost?

4. Each of the four options can be gamed in turn. For Option 2's outcome index in particular, describe how a determined area sales manager would improve unique outlets billed and retailer callback confirmation without improving coverage — and say what you would measure against that.

5. The August 2023 clause pays Nakshaa more when a number it computes goes up. Suppose the board accepts that this structure must end. What does Nakshaa sell instead, what happens to the New Jersey pipeline and the Kanz expansion, and what is the strongest argument that the clause was never the real problem?

6. It is Monday morning. Siddharth has ninety minutes, ₹26 crore of cash, a methodology frozen by contract until March 2027, a Dubai confirmation due on the 15th, a data scientist who will not certify his central number, and a salesman in Solapur who showed him the gaming without embarrassment because everyone already knows. What does he propose, what does he tell Shubhankar and when, what does he stop measuring — and what does he say to the two directors in the room when one of them asks whether the last eight quarters of earned bonus should be given back?

11. Sunday night, continued

At 12.20 a.m. Siddharth opened the paper and changed the title of the first slide from "Visit Integrity: options" to "What our number is measuring", and then changed it back, because the second title was an accusation and he did not yet know whom he was accusing.

He took out Pawar's log again. Thirty-nine productive calls; 22 shops entered; the app's own telemetry, which he had pulled on Saturday night, showed eleven visits with dwell times between 41 and 46 seconds and one sync burst of nine records at 6.52 p.m. On Ritika's model, Pawar's day was flagged. On Shubhankar's leaderboard, it was a good day — better than average. On the reading Siddharth could not stop returning to, Pawar had done the twenty-two visits that the day contained and had then, at no cost to anyone's sales, satisfied an instruction that could not be satisfied honestly.

At the bottom of the last page, under the two lines he had shown nobody, he wrote a third: whatever we put on the slide, write down the number that would tell us it has stopped being true — and who has to look at it, and how often. He did not write what that number would be. Outside, the first of the pre-monsoon winds was moving through the gulmohar on the lane, and the steering committee was in nine hours.

Counter-metrics and Goodhart's Law

A near-expert treatment: the formal anatomy of measure corruption, why guardrails are almost always underpowered, and what competent practitioners still disagree about.

1. Two decisions, one week apart

On 3 February 2026, Ira Khandelwal, VP of product at Tilori, a Mumbai direct-to-consumer beauty and personal-care app doing about ₹95 crore a quarter, sat in a growth review with a number she had asked for and now distrusted. Repeat purchase rate within 30 days — Tilori's headline target since October — had gone from 24.1% to 31.6%. The mechanism was a reorder rail shipped in November: a home-screen strip that reassembled a customer's last basket in one tap. The board deck already had the number in it. What Ira had noticed three days earlier, by accident, was that return rate on rail-originated baskets was 9.4% against 4.1% for hand-built ones, and that Tilori's returns are not free: reverse logistics in a category of liquids and seals costs roughly ₹210 an order, and a returned mascara is written off rather than restocked. Nobody had agreed in advance what return rate would disqualify the rail, because the rail had been scoped as a convenience feature rather than a growth bet, and convenience features at Tilori did not get guardrails.

Eight days later and 850 kilometres away, Prakash Venugopal, general manager of claims at Sampige Health Cloud, a Bengaluru enterprise SaaS firm selling revenue-cycle software to about 140 private hospital groups, faced the mirror image. Its flagship module, Suchak, auto-adjudicates claims against payer rules; the contractual metric in eleven of its largest agreements is straight-through processing rate, moved from 61% to 78% in two quarters. Prakash's counter-metric existed, was reviewed weekly, and had not moved at all: denial-overturn rate — claims auto-approved by Suchak and later reversed by the payer — sat at 2.9%, statistically flat. He did not believe it. Payer audits in the Indian private-insurance market run on a six-to-nine-month lag, and his largest customer's finance head had mentioned in passing an unusual volume of queries on cataract packages. Prakash's counter-metric was not silent because nothing was wrong. It was silent because it could not yet have spoken.

The two cases bracket the subject. Ira has a target and no guardrail. Prakash has a guardrail structurally incapable of catching the harm it was chosen for, which is worse, because it manufactures confidence. What follows is why both situations are common, what the formal structure underneath them is, and where experienced practitioners still part company.

2. The idea, its history, and who disagrees about it

A target metric is a quantity a team is held to. A counter-metric is a second quantity, chosen before the work begins, whose movement would indicate the target was moved through the mechanism the organisation did not want. It is a specific kind of guardrail: guardrails protect anything you care about; counter-metrics are chosen adversarially, against a named exploit.

The lineage has three roots that are frequently conflated. Charles Goodhart, writing for the Reserve Bank of Australia in 1975 about UK monetary policy, observed that a statistical regularity tends to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control — a claim about the instability of an observed relationship. Donald Campbell, in 1976, made the sociological claim: the more an indicator is used for social decision-making, the more it corrupts the processes it monitors. Robert Lucas's 1976 critique made the econometric version: parameters estimated under one policy regime cannot evaluate another, because agents re-optimise. Marilyn Strathern's 1997 gloss — "when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure" — is the one product managers quote, and the loosest of the four.

The distinction matters operationally because of a taxonomy that David Manheim and Scott Garrabrant set out in 2018, which is the single most useful piece of formal work available to a practitioner. They separate four mechanisms by which optimising a proxy diverges from the goal. Regressional Goodhart: the proxy equals the goal plus noise, so selecting hard on the proxy selects partly on the noise — the winner's curse. Extremal: the proxy-goal relationship held in the observed range and simply does not hold at the extreme you have now pushed into. Causal: the correlation was real but non-causal, so intervening on the proxy does not move the goal. Adversarial: an agent with different interests deliberately exploits your use of the proxy. These need different remedies, and treating them as one phenomenon is the most common error among otherwise strong practitioners.

Figure 1. The four divergence mechanisms after Manheim and Garrabrant (2018). The remedies are not interchangeable: replication fixes regressional Goodhart and does nothing for adversarial Goodhart; an adversarially chosen counter-metric will not notice that a relationship simply stopped holding at the tail.

Three schools of thought disagree about what follows from all this. The abolitionist school descends from W. Edwards Deming, whose eleventh management point was to eliminate numerical quotas: a target under pressure is irredeemable, and the answer is to manage the system, not the number. It would sign "numerical targets attached to appraisal reliably corrupt behaviour," and would not sign "a well-chosen counter-metric restores the target's validity" — to this school, a guardrail is a second thing to game.

The experimentation school, from the controlled-experiment literature of Ron Kohavi, Diane Tang and Ya Xu and institutionalised in large platform metric stacks, holds that the problem is statistical and tractable: define an overall evaluation criterion, attach automated degradation checks, block shipping when they trip. It would sign "guardrails must be pre-registered, powered and automatically enforced," and would reject both "abandon targets" and "judgement may override a tripped guardrail."

The stewardship school — the working position of most senior product leaders, articulated more in practice than in print — holds that metrics are inputs to judgement and that the counter-metric's job is to force a named human into a decision on the record. It would sign "every metric needs an owner, a cadence and the decision it informs," and would not sign "a threshold breach should automatically block a launch," believing automatic gates get negotiated around rather than obeyed.

3. Mechanics in depth, including the arithmetic nobody runs

Expert practice has five steps, of which the middle three are usually left implicit.

Adversarial pre-mortem. Before shipping, the team writes down how it would move the target with no real improvement. Ira's team, doing this retrospectively, produced four: surface the rail on baskets the customer had already abandoned; mix consumable and non-consumable items indiscriminately; pre-tick a subscription box; and count a reorder complete at payment rather than delivery. Three of the four had in fact shipped.

Mechanism-proximate selection. The counter-metric must sit causally downstream of the named exploit, not merely be a number about quality. Tilori's satisfaction score is a quality metric; return rate on rail-originated baskets is mechanism-proximate, because every one of the four exploits raises it.

Power analysis — the step almost universally skipped. This is where Prakash's guardrail failed. A target is chosen because a large movement is expected; a counter-metric matters at small ones. Suppose the baseline denial-overturn rate is 2.9% and the smallest harmful shift Sampige would want to act on is 0.5 percentage points. For a two-proportion test at 80% power and a two-sided 5% level, the required sample per arm is approximately 16 × p(1−p) / δ², which here gives 16 × 0.029 × 0.971 / 0.005², or about 18,000 claims per arm. Sampige processes roughly 42,000 claims a month across the affected cohort, so with a clean split the test is adequately powered in about three weeks — except that the outcome is only observed after payer adjudication, which lags six to nine months. The metric is powered; the observation window is not. Prakash's flat 2.9% describes claims filed last July.

Figure 2. Guardrail sensitivity is the binding constraint. A counter-metric with a low base rate needs an order of magnitude more data than the target it protects, because it must detect a small absolute shift rather than a large relative one.

Threshold setting and the multiplicity problem. Once a team runs several guardrails, false alarms compound: with twenty independent checks at a 5% level, the probability of at least one spurious trip is 1 − 0.95²⁰ ≈ 64%. Teams that see this twice stop believing guardrails at all, the worst equilibrium available. The disciplined fixes are to run guardrails as one-sided non-inferiority tests against an explicit harm margin rather than two-sided tests against zero; to tighten the level on the full battery while keeping the mechanism-proximate counter-metrics at conventional levels; and to require confirmation across two consecutive cycles before a trip becomes a decision.

Ownership binding. The pair must be reviewed in one meeting, on one cadence, by someone with standing to stop the work. Sampige reviewed denial-overturn rate in a Tuesday customer-success forum and straight-through rate in a Thursday product forum, with no shared attendee below the general manager. That organisational fact, not any statistical one, is why the observation-lag problem went unnoticed for two quarters.

4. When the discipline applies, stated as testable claims

Four conditions determine whether a counter-metric earns its cost. Each can be checked rather than debated.

Claim one: the target is under enough optimisation pressure to bend. Test: does anyone's compensation, promotion case or public commitment depend on it? Tilori's repeat rate sat in the board deck and the growth team's bonus; Sampige's straight-through rate is written into contracts with service credits attached, which is higher pressure still. A metric watched by nobody needs no counter-metric, and instrumenting one wastes review time the metrics under real pressure need.

Claim two: there exists a cheap action that moves the target without moving the goal. Test: can you name it in one sentence? For Tilori, yes — surface the rail to customers who had already rejected the basket. For Sampige, the honest answer is subtler: the cheap action was loosening the confidence threshold at which Suchak auto-approves, which is a single configuration value that no engineer considered a product decision.

Claim three: the harm is observable inside the decision window. Where the answer is no, the idea is actively misleading. Sampige's harm appears only after payer audit, and a counter-metric that cannot report before the decision is a post-mortem, not a guardrail. The move is not a better lagging metric but a leading surrogate — for Sampige, the rate at which auto-approved claims fall below the historical confidence band, measurable on the day of filing — plus explicit acceptance that the surrogate is itself a proxy with its own Goodhart exposure.

Claim four: someone can act on a breach. Test: name the person and the action. If the rollout cannot be reverted — a hardware revision, an announced price, a contractual commitment — the counter-metric buys information for the next decision, not this one, and should be resourced accordingly rather than reviewed as though it were a brake.

5. Hard edge cases and what happens at the seams

In multi-product companies the counter-metric is frequently another team's target, converting a measurement question into a political one. Cannibalisation is the standard case: a growth team's activation target is guarded by a revenue team's order-value target, and the two meet only at a leadership review where each defends its own number. Mature companies handle this less elegantly than they claim: the real answer is usually a single metric owner one level above both, with a pre-agreed rule about which number wins, rather than the "aligned incentives" the org chart describes.

In two-sided marketplaces the counter-metric is structurally the other side's welfare. Sajha Mandi, an agri marketplace linking Nashik and Belagavi growers to institutional buyers, targets listing-approval speed; the counter-metric is buyer rejection on delivery, because the cheapest way to approve faster is to approve worse. The seam is that the two sides have different latencies — approval in minutes, rejection three days later — so the guardrail must be indexed by cohort rather than calendar week, or the rate looks flat while quality falls.

In regulated products the tension is sharper than most writing admits. A counter-metric is, by design, contemporaneous documentation that the firm anticipated a specific harm. In insurance and lending, where the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority of India and the Reserve Bank of India both expect boards to evidence conduct oversight, that documentation is an asset in an examination and a liability in a dispute. Firms that handle it well route the measurement into an established conduct-risk framework, review it with legal present, and set thresholds that trigger investigation rather than conclusions. Firms that handle it badly stop writing thresholds down.

In hardware-plus-software, feedback latency dominates. Tamarai Devices, a Coimbatore maker of connected water purifiers, targets filter-replacement compliance, since replacements carry its margin. The cheap exploit is tightening the firmware's "replace now" trigger; the counter-metric — premature-replacement rate from residual-capacity telemetry — exists, but the real harm, customers concluding the device nags and churning at renewal, appears eleven months later. Hardware organisations compensate with staged geographic rollouts and retained control cohorts, accepting revenue forgone as the price of an interpretable signal.

In AI-native products the problem changes in kind rather than degree. Ujjwal Lending, a Chennai credit platform, optimises an underwriting model, Tarka, against approval-rate-at-fixed-loss-rate. A human team games a metric in ways a human can anticipate; an optimiser searches a far larger space and finds exploits nobody wrote in the pre-mortem — the specification-gaming literature catalogues dozens. Two practices follow. Counter-metrics for model-optimised targets must include a measure of distributional change — applicant mix, feature drift, subgroup approval spread — because the exploit shows first as a shift in who is served rather than as headline degradation. And the set must be refreshed each retraining cycle, since a fixed guardrail becomes part of the environment the optimiser adapts to.

6. What separates an expert from a competent practitioner

The expert diagnoses which Goodhart is operating before choosing a remedy. The tell is the first question asked: not "what should the guardrail be" but "which of the four mechanisms is this." Regressional Goodhart wants replication and shrinkage; adversarial wants a mechanism-proximate counter-metric; extremal wants a range limit. Prescribing a counter-metric for regressional decay treats a statistical artefact as bad faith, which poisons the team relationship and does not fix the number.

The expert treats guardrail silence as an unresolved question, not a clean bill of health. The obvious reading of a flat counter-metric is that nothing is wrong. The expert asks its minimum detectable effect and whether the observation window covers the period under review. Prakash's instinct is the most valuable behaviour in this topic: he distrusted a number telling him what he wanted to hear.

The expert knows the risk profile changes over a target's life. Early gains are usually honest, because real headroom remains; gaming risk rises as a target nears its natural ceiling and the remaining moves turn structural. The tell is a team reviewing guardrails on fixed cadence at fixed thresholds across a twelve-month programme, as though the hazard rate were constant. It is not.

The expert refuses to incentivise the counter-metric while keeping someone accountable for looking at it. The distinction is fine and frequently botched. Pay someone to keep return rate low and returns become exchanges; hold someone accountable for presenting return rate honestly each cycle and you get the behaviour you want. The tell is a bonus line naming the guardrail.

The expert distinguishes gaming from a change in the population. Tilori's return rate rose partly because the rail was used disproportionately by newer customers, whose returns were always higher; a segment-blind comparison would attribute a mix effect to a design flaw. The tell is an expert who asks for the guardrail split by cohort before accepting its headline movement in either direction.

The expert anticipates displacement. A counter-metric does not remove the pressure that produced gaming; it redirects it toward whatever remains unmeasured. Once Tilori watches returns, the next adaptation is pushing customers toward non-returnable categories. The tell is an expert who asks, at adoption, where the pressure will go next — and schedules a review of that, rather than declaring the problem solved.

The expert knows when the counter-metric is a constraint rather than a watched number. Some harms are not tradeable at any rate — a safety threshold, a regulatory limit, a consent requirement — and modelling them as guardrails invites negotiation. The tell is language: "this is a constraint, the programme does not proceed," not "our guardrail is slightly elevated."

The expert is unimpressed by guardrail coverage statistics. "Ninety per cent of our OKRs have counter-metrics" describes a compliance exercise. The relevant number is how often in the last year a guardrail changed a decision. If the answer is zero across dozens of launches, either the organisation is unusually virtuous or the guardrails are decorative, and the base rate favours the second.

7. How it differs by product type and company stage

In consumer products the exploit is nearly always friction removal, the harm post-purchase, and the loop fast enough that weekly review works. In B2B and enterprise the exploit is threshold loosening or scope redefinition and the harm surfaces at renewal or audit, quarters later, so the counter-metric needs a leading surrogate. In platforms and marketplaces the counter-metric is the other side's outcome and the difficulty is cohort indexing across mismatched latencies. In hardware you cannot roll back atoms, so guardrails pay for themselves through staged rollout rather than reversal. In AI products they must cover distributional change and be refreshed every training cycle.

Where the difference is overstated: choosing which counter-metric to use is not meaningfully different across sectors — in every case it is the number downstream of the named cheap action. What differs is latency, reversibility and who owns the data: three logistical facts, not three philosophies.

Stage changes the practice more than sector does. A thirty-person company sees its whole system and catches gaming in conversation; its risk is having no target sharp enough to concentrate effort. At a few hundred people the failure is the seam — the counter-metric exists, on another team's dashboard, reviewed on another day, which is Sampige's situation exactly. At thousands the failure inverts: batteries grow so large that multiplicity produces constant false alarms, teams discount them, and the problem becomes restoring signal by cutting back to a few mechanism-proximate metrics with real thresholds.

8. Three worked examples, including one that failed

Tilori, consumer, partial success. Ira's team re-cut the data by cohort. Repeat rate rose 7.5 points overall; among customers with more than three prior orders it rose 9.1 points with return rate up only 1.2 points, while among first-and-second-order customers repeat rate rose 4.4 points and return rate rose 8.9 points. Priced at ₹210 per return over 480,000 quarterly rail-originated orders, the incremental returns cost about ₹2.6 crore a quarter, against incremental contribution from genuine repeats of roughly ₹5.1 crore. Net positive — but concentrated entirely in the experienced cohort. The rail was retained for customers with three or more orders and withdrawn below that line, which cost 2.1 points of the headline number and improved net contribution by an estimated ₹1.7 crore a quarter.

Sajha Mandi, marketplace, success through cohort indexing. Listing-approval time fell from 41 minutes to 9. Buyer rejection rate, measured by calendar week, stayed at 6.2% and looked reassuring. Re-indexed by listing cohort — rejections attributed to the week of approval rather than the week of rejection — the rate for listings approved after the change was 9.8%. On 74,000 monthly consignments at ₹1,450 per rejection in re-routing and spoilage, that 3.6-point gap was about ₹38 lakh a month, against a working-capital benefit of roughly ₹22 lakh. Manual review was reinstated for first-time sellers only, recovering most of the speed gain at a fraction of the cost.

Tapri Bazaar, quick commerce, failure and recovery. Tapri targeted delivery promise accuracy and paired it with a guardrail — average order value — chosen because it was already on the dashboard. The exploit was to narrow the catalogue shown to riders in congested zones, which improved promise accuracy from 88% to 96% and depressed selection for about 11% of customers. Average order value moved 0.3%, well inside noise; with roughly 9,000 orders a day in affected zones and a ₹40 standard deviation on a ₹480 mean, the guardrail could only have detected a shift above about ₹2.6, and the true effect was smaller and slower. Eight months later, order frequency in those zones was down 14% against control, a run-rate loss estimated at ₹11 crore a year. Recovery took two quarters: the guardrail became catalogue-coverage-at-order-time — mechanism-proximate and observable the same day — a 5% permanent holdout was instituted in every affected zone, and the launch review template was changed to require a stated minimum detectable effect for every guardrail. The organisational fix mattered more than the metric fix, which alone would have been re-broken by the next team.

9. Failure modes, early warning signs and the cost of lateness

The available-rather-than-proximate guardrail announces itself when a team produces its guardrail instantly from an existing dashboard. Diagnostic: "which cheap action would move this number?" Caught early it costs an afternoon of metric definition; caught late it costs a Tapri — eight months of undetected harm at a run-rate in crores.

The underpowered guardrail announces itself as a suspiciously stable number during a period of large change. Diagnostic: "what is the smallest shift this could detect at our volumes, and does the observation window cover this quarter?" Caught early it costs a longer measurement period; caught late it produces confident false assurance, which is more expensive than no guardrail because it suppresses the qualitative signals people would otherwise raise.

The unowned guardrail shows up as a metric reviewed in a different forum from its target. Diagnostic: "when did the person who can stop this work last see both numbers together?" Caught early it costs a calendar change; caught late it costs the credibility of the measurement practice, because the post-mortem always reveals the data existed.

The thresholdless guardrail shows up as a first-time argument about whether a movement is bad enough to matter, conducted under launch pressure. Diagnostic: "what number, agreed in writing beforehand, would have forced this conversation a month ago?" Caught late, the decision goes to whoever is most senior in the room rather than to the evidence.

The incentivised guardrail shows up as both numbers improving in implausible harmony. Diagnostic: "does anyone's variable pay depend on this number's level?" Caught late it produces two corrupted metrics and an organisation that no longer knows what is true about its product.

10. Where competent experts genuinely disagree

Automatic gates versus advisory signals. The experimentation school's case is empirical: at platform scale, automated degradation checks catch regressions human review misses, and every discretionary override becomes a negotiation won by whoever holds the most political capital. The stewardship case is that hard gates produce threshold management — teams design changes to land just inside the limit, Goodhart applied to the guardrail itself — and that a gate nobody can override is routed around by relabelling the launch. Settling it would require override and post-launch regression rates compared across organisations under both regimes; nobody has published that.

Composite criterion versus explicit pair. One camp folds harm into a single weighted evaluation criterion, on the grounds that an explicit weight forces the trade-off to be made once, in the open, rather than re-litigated per launch. The other holds that a composite hides the trade-off: a large gain can mathematically swamp a serious harm, and the weights are set by people who will not bear it. For the composite position to be wrong, harms would have to be non-tradeable near their thresholds — which for safety and conduct harms is plainly true, and is why most composite advocates carve those out.

Whether counter-metrics should carry incentives. The majority view is no. The minority view, from balanced-scorecard practice, is that an unincentivised metric is one nobody will defend against a quarter-end revenue push, so the real choice is between a corrupted guardrail and an ignored one. Its evidence: where nothing depends on the guardrail, guardrail-driven launch delays are close to nonexistent.

The abolitionist challenge. Deming's descendants hold that the entire apparatus is a workaround for a bad idea — that targets attached to appraisal should be replaced by process capability measurement and continuous improvement. Its evidence is that the failure modes above recur across sectors and decades despite universal awareness of Goodhart's Law — what you would expect if the problem were structural rather than technique-deficient. For it to be wrong, organisations would have to sustain focus without numerical targets; honestly, a few can, most cannot, and nobody has a theory of which is which.

Two questions remain unsettled: how to choose thresholds by any principle other than precedent and negotiation, and whether guardrail batteries should be standardised across an organisation — comparable and cheap, but by construction not mechanism-proximate — or bespoke per launch, the opposite trade.

11. What mastery looks like

Someone who has merely studied this produces a guardrail column in the launch template. Someone who has internalised it behaves differently in four visible ways. They ask about the exploit before the metric, because the metric is downstream of the exploit. They interrogate flat guardrails harder than moving ones, since a moving guardrail is doing its job and a flat one may be doing nothing. They price both sides in a common currency and argue about the conversion rate rather than about whether a chart looks concerning. And they treat the wiring — one owner, one meeting, one pre-agreed threshold, one person with standing to stop the work — as the substance of the practice rather than its overhead, because in every documented failure the data existed and the wiring did not.

12. What Ira and Prakash decided

Ira presented both numbers to the board with the cohort split visible, recommended withdrawing the rail below three prior orders, and accepted a restatement of headline repeat rate from 31.6% to 29.5%. Her reasoning: the restatement was survivable now and would not be in two quarters, once returns had compounded and someone else had found the cohort effect first. She also ruled that any feature shipped into a metric under board commitment requires a stated exploit and a mechanism-proximate counter-metric, whatever it is scoped as.

Prakash did not stop the rollout. He instead commissioned a same-day surrogate — the share of auto-approved claims falling below Suchak's historical confidence band — reconstructed the last two quarters against it, and found the share had risen from 4% to 17% in the window where straight-through rate had improved most. He disclosed the surrogate and the reconstruction to his three largest hospital customers before their audits surfaced it, on the judgement that a supplier who brings you the problem retains the contract and a supplier whose problem you discover does not. Whether that judgement was correct is not yet known; two of the three renewals fall due in August.

Discussion questions

1. Sampige's counter-metric was correctly chosen, correctly owned and correctly reviewed, and was still useless. What generalisable rule does that suggest about the relationship between a counter-metric's validity and its latency, and how would you write that rule into a launch template without making the template unusable?

2. Ira's cohort analysis rescued the programme, but she found it by accident. What would have had to be true about Tilori's review practice for the cohort split to be visible in week two rather than week eleven — and what does that practice cost per launch at Tilori's size?

3. The abolitionist position holds that both companies' problems originate in having numerical targets at all. Construct the strongest version of that argument for Tilori specifically, then identify what Tilori would lose if it adopted it.

13. Going deeper

  1. Guardrail metrics — the general category this topic specialises; the full battery clarifies why mechanism-proximate counter-metrics must be a small, deliberately chosen subset of it.
  2. Velocity, throughput and what not to measure — the same corruption dynamic applied to engineering output, where the measured quantity is furthest from the thing anyone actually wants.
  3. What makes a good metric — sensitivity, stability and attributability decide whether a counter-metric can detect harm in time.
  4. Vanity vs actionable metrics — most decorative guardrails are vanity metrics wearing a safety label; this distinction is the fastest test.
  5. GAME framework — gives the structure in which targets and their counter-metrics are declared together rather than bolted on after scoping.
  6. Acquisition, retention, monetisation actions — maps which lever a target sits on, which is how you predict where displaced pressure surfaces next.
  7. Direct vs proxy, magnitude vs ratio — the proxy-goal gap is the substrate of regressional and extremal Goodhart, and ratios hide the cohort mix effects that nearly cost Tilori its programme.
  8. North Star metric — the highest-pressure target in any organisation, so the one whose counter-metric deserves the most adversarial selection and frequent refresh.

Kaamkaaj: The Placement That Counted Twice

Gurugram, August 2025. A hiring marketplace has beaten its placement target by a third. Its head of product has four days to work out what the number is actually measuring.

1. Monday morning, Sector 44

At nine on Monday, 4 August 2025, Ira Sabharwal walked into Kaamkaaj's office on the eighth floor of a tower in Sector 44, Gurugram, with a printout she had made at home and had not shown to anyone. On Friday the 8th she would sit in the quarterly business review and be asked one question by the board: could Kaamkaaj hold its Q3 target of 1.4 lakh verified placements a month through the festive hiring ramp into Diwali? July had come in at 1.43 lakh, and on the strength of that the answer should have taken four seconds.

The printout was a cohort table her data scientist had sent from Toronto at 2 a.m. Indian time. It said that of the workers Kaamkaaj had placed in May, only 41 per cent were still at the same employer on day thirty. In February the figure had been 58 per cent. Nobody had changed what Kaamkaaj sold, or who it sold to, or the roles it filled. In May it had changed one thing: how a placement got confirmed.

2. Kaamkaaj

Kaamkaaj was founded in 2020 to fix a specific Indian labour-market problem: the gap between the enormous number of people looking for delivery, warehouse, retail-floor, security and field-sales work, and the enormous number of employers who needed them at two weeks' notice and had no way to find them. By mid-2025 it had 62 lakh registered workers, about 11,000 active employers, and on-ground operations in fourteen cities. Its largest categories were last-mile delivery, quick-commerce dark-store staffing and organised retail — which in practice meant that the demand side of its business rose and fell with the hiring plans of Swiggy, Zomato, Zepto, Flipkart and Reliance Retail, and with the hundreds of third-party manpower contractors who staffed on their behalf.

Kaamkaaj charged per placement. A self-serve employer paid ₹1,100 for a delivery-rider placement and up to ₹2,800 for a store-supervisor role; enterprise accounts bought annual blocks at negotiated rates. Revenue in FY25 was about ₹214 crore. It competed with Apna, WorkIndia and the blue-collar arms of the established job portals, and its pitch to employers had always been the same: not the largest database, but the highest ratio of candidates who actually turn up and stay.

That pitch made "verified placement" the most important word in the company. A placement counted — and was billed — when it was confirmed as a genuine joining. Until May 2025, confirmation required the employer's hiring coordinator to log in to the Kaamkaaj dashboard, find the candidate and mark a joining date, or a Kaamkaaj field associate to submit a signed joining slip. Both were slow. Roughly 19 per cent of genuine joinings were never confirmed at all, which meant Kaamkaaj was under-billing and, worse, could not tell employers how well it was performing.

3. What changed in May

The fix was designed by Lena Hoffmann, Kaamkaaj's product designer in Berlin, and shipped on 12 May. It was elegant and it was obviously correct. Confirmation moved to WhatsApp: the coordinator received a message listing the candidates sent that week and confirmed joinings with one tap each. Where an employer had no coordinator, Kaamkaaj's own field associate could confirm from the app after a site visit. Unconfirmed placements now escalated automatically after 72 hours, and a placement left unconfirmed for seven days could be marked joined by the field associate on the strength of a photograph of the worker at the site.

Confirmed placements in June were 1.37 lakh, up 34 per cent on April. Rajat Khurana, who ran growth and supply, called it the highest-return two-week build in the company's history, and by the numbers he had he was right. Nothing in the funnel he watched looked wrong. Candidates sent per employer were flat. Interview-to-offer ratios were flat. Cost of acquiring a worker was down, because the same worker could now be placed with less friction.

What Meghna Rao noticed in Toronto in late July was that the same worker was being placed rather often. Nine per cent of July's placements were of workers who had already been placed twice or more in the preceding ninety days. In February the figure had been 3 per cent. A worker joined a dark store, was confirmed, left in eleven days, was contacted again by the same field associate, joined another dark store two kilometres away, and was confirmed again. Two placements, two invoices, one worker who had not found stable work and two employers who had each paid ₹1,100 for a vacancy that was open again inside a fortnight.

Exhibit 1 is the panel Ira assembled over the weekend from four different systems. The first row is the number the board tracks. The rest are numbers nobody had been asked to report.

5. The people

Rajat Khurana, VP Growth and Supply, Gurugram. Rajat carries the placement number, and so do the 340 field associates in his line and the ₹90-per-joining incentive they earn. He believes the retention decline is a labour-market story, not a product story: quick-commerce hiring in the first half of 2025 was frantic, attrition across the industry was terrible, and Kaamkaaj is being blamed for a churn it did not create. He wants the target held and the festive ramp prioritised. He is also aware, though he has not said it, that his team's variable pay for Q3 is built on 1.4 lakh a month.

Meghna Rao, Senior Data Scientist, Toronto. Meghna built the cohort analysis and is the only person who has looked at the confirmation-source field. Her position is that the placement metric stopped measuring placements on 12 May and that the company should say so plainly. Working ten and a half hours behind Gurugram, she has been in exactly one of the six meetings where this was discussed, and her memo has been read by three people.

Priya Balakrishnan, Customer Success Lead, Singapore. Priya owns the enterprise book, including Al Waha Facilities Group in Dubai, which hires housekeeping and security staff from Kerala and Uttar Pradesh through Kaamkaaj and is up for renewal on 30 September at ₹3.6 crore. Al Waha's operations director has already raised two escalations about workers who did not complete their first month. Priya wants the day-30 measure made contractual before renewal, because she would rather negotiate a lower placement count than defend a number the client can disprove.

Karan Mehta, Head of Sales, New Jersey. Karan sells to the India operations of American retail and logistics companies, and his pipeline for the next two quarters is ₹22 crore. His pitch leans on scale — placements per month is the slide that closes deals. He is sceptical of changing the headline number four weeks before a board meeting and three months before a funding conversation, and he has said, reasonably, that no competitor reports a thirty-day sustained-placement figure, so Kaamkaaj would be marking itself down against a benchmark nobody else uses.

6. The options

Option A: hold the target, report both numbers. Keep the definition and the incentive, add day-30 retention and the re-placement rate to the monthly pack as monitoring, and revisit in January. Upside: no disruption to the festive ramp, no awkward board conversation, Karan's pipeline intact, and if Rajat is right about the labour market the numbers will recover on their own. Cost: the dispute line is compounding at roughly ₹14 lakh a month, the enterprise renewal is exposed, and the counter-metrics have no threshold, which means in practice they will be narrated and not acted upon.

Option B: change the metric of record. Define a placement as a joining where the worker is still employed on day thirty, verified against employer payroll or a worker-confirmed first salary credit. Re-baseline Q3 to roughly 92,000 a month, rewrite the field incentive to pay on day-30 survival rather than on joining, and move enterprise billing to the same basis. Upside: the number means what it says, and the company's differentiating claim becomes measurable. Cost: an immediate 36 per cent optical drop, a thirty-day lag in every operating report and in every field associate's pay cycle, a revenue-recognition and invoicing change that finance estimates at six weeks of work, and Karan's point about benchmarks stands.

Option C: keep the target, attach thresholds and independent verification. Placements continue to be counted on joining, but three counter-metrics get pre-agreed lines and an owner outside growth: day-30 retention not below 52 per cent, re-placement-within-90-days not above 4 per cent, and enterprise dispute cost not above ₹30 lakh a month. Confirmation by Kaamkaaj's own staff is capped at 25 per cent of placements and requires a second signal — an employer roster entry or a worker-confirmed salary credit. The field incentive is held for thirty days and forfeited if the worker leaves. A breach of any line for two consecutive months triggers an automatic move to Option B. Upside: the festive ramp is not disturbed, the loop is closed at the point where it is created, and the decision rule exists before the argument. Cost: it is more complex to explain, the second confirmation signal needs engineering work in Bengaluru and Pune that is currently committed to festive capacity, and it leaves the headline number reported on a basis Ira already believes is inflated.

7. Questions for discussion

1. Reconstruct what happened between 12 May and 31 July. Which of the changes shipped in May created the re-placement loop, and which merely made it visible?

2. Exhibit 1 shows six numbers moving together. Which of them are counter-metrics in the strict sense — derived from a specific way the placement target could be hit cheaply — and which are simply other things that happen to have got worse?

3. Rajat's labour-market explanation is not obviously wrong. What evidence in the case supports it, what evidence tells against it, and what single additional analysis would settle it?

4. What should Ira recommend on Friday, and what exactly should she say to the board about the July figure of 1.43 lakh?

8. A note for the learner

This case is an instance of Goodhart's law in its most ordinary form. Kaamkaaj's placement count was a good measure for five years precisely because it was hard to produce: confirmation required effort from a party with no stake in the number. The May release removed that friction and, in doing so, handed the pen to people who were paid per signature. Nobody cheated. A field associate who re-contacts a worker who has just left a dark store is doing something defensible, even kind. But the act became newly profitable, its volume changed, and the number stopped standing for the thing it used to stand for.

The lens to bring is the derivation, not the dashboard. Start from the target, ask how a rational person could move it without doing the work, and let each route name its own detector. Here the routes are short: confirm placements you are paid to confirm; re-place the same worker; never record a departure. Their detectors are the confirmation-source share, the re-placement rate, and day-30 retention — and notice that the confirmation-source field is the one that points directly at the mechanism, while day-30 retention only shows the damage a month later. A good answer distinguishes the leading trace from the lagging confirmation, and notices that Kaamkaaj's most useful counter-metric was already being logged and had never been looked at.

A well-reasoned answer also takes the independence question seriously. Any measure of retention that depends on the employer coordinator's diligence, or on the field associate's report, is measured by the party under scrutiny. That is why the verification signal in Option C matters more than the threshold: a worker-confirmed first salary credit, or a roster entry pulled from an enterprise client's own system, is a trace the interested party cannot author.

One defensible path is Option C, with a stated intention to move to Option B in January. The reasoning runs like this. Ira does not need to win the argument about whether the labour market or the product caused the decline — she needs a decision rule that resolves it either way, and Option C supplies one: if Rajat is right, retention recovers as festive hiring normalises and no lines are breached; if Meghna is right, two months of breach converts the metric automatically and nobody has to be proved wrong in a meeting. The escrowed field incentive removes the loop at its source at a cost of ₹90 per joining held for thirty days, which is small against ₹61 lakh of monthly disputes. Priya gets what she needs for Al Waha, because a threshold on day-30 retention is something she can put in a renewal conversation even before it is in the contract. And Karan's benchmark objection is answered honestly: Kaamkaaj continues to report placements on the industry basis while telling the board, in the same pack, what proportion of them survive a month.

What Option C does not do is make the headline number true, and a learner should be able to say why that is a real cost rather than a rhetorical one. Every month Kaamkaaj reports 1.4 lakh placements is a month in which the field organisation, the sales pipeline and the board's expectations are being calibrated against a figure that includes roughly 13,000 re-placements of workers who did not stay. Deferring the redefinition to January buys operating stability through Diwali and buys the argument a factual resolution; it also makes the eventual correction larger. That trade is the decision, and it is a judgement rather than a calculation.

Counter-metrics and Goodhart's Law

Every target gets gamed. The discipline is knowing how, and building a second gauge that would tell you.

1. The eleven-second checkout

On the morning of 14 August 2025, Radhika Menon, head of product for checkout at Belani Retail — a Bengaluru-based online grocery platform doing roughly ₹340 crore a month in gross merchandise value — was looking at a chart she had been chasing for a quarter. Average checkout time, from "tap pay" to "order confirmed," had fallen from 34 seconds to 11. That had been her team's objective since May, cut latency by 60%, because Belani's funnel data showed every extra five seconds cost roughly 1.8% of completed carts, worth an estimated ₹6 lakh a day at current volumes.

Her VP wanted to announce the 11-second number at the September town hall as proof the quarter's engineering spend had paid off. Radhika was not ready to sign off. Support tickets tagged "wrong item delivered" or "double-charged" had risen 22% over the same ten weeks, though nobody on her team tracked that number against checkout — it lived on a different dashboard, owned by operations. She had also watched a session recording where a customer, mid-checkout, was auto-selected into a saved address and payment method neither had reviewed, and the order closed in nine seconds untouched. The speed was real; whether the transaction was still well-formed was a question nobody's dashboard was built to ask. Her decision, due before the town hall, was whether to declare success, hold the number back, or pause the rollout. The stakes were not hypothetical: a competitor, Ferro Mart, had shipped a similarly aggressive one-tap checkout eight months earlier and quietly rolled it back after a spike in disputes reported through the National Payments Corporation of India's channel.

2. The idea

A target metric is the number a team is told to move — checkout time, activation rate, tickets resolved per hour. A counter-metric (also called a guardrail metric) is a second number, chosen in advance, that tracks the harm a team could plausibly do while chasing the target — one that moves if the team "wins" the target the wrong way. The pairing exists because of Goodhart's Law, after Charles Goodhart, a Bank of England economist who wrote in 1975, in the context of UK monetary policy, that any observed statistical regularity collapses once pressure is placed on it for control. The anthropologist Marilyn Strathern restated it in 1997 as the line practitioners now quote: "When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure." Goodhart was describing central banks targeting a measure of money supply and watching banks reclassify liabilities to keep hitting the number while the actual policy goal slipped away. The same mechanism hit Belani: speed stopped correlating with "good checkout" once speed itself became the graded objective, because the fastest way to get faster was removing verification steps that had been quietly doing useful work.

The sentence Radhika could say in the town hall without sounding glib is this: "Every target we set creates an incentive to win it in ways we didn't intend, so no target ships without a counter-metric that would catch the cheapest way to fake it." It names the risk honestly and commits the team to a concrete practice, not a vague caution.

3. How the pairing is actually built

The mechanics are not exotic, but three steps are usually skipped, and that is where most counter-metric programmes fail quietly.

Step one — name the target's cheapest failure mode before shipping. A team asks: if I wanted to move this number without real work, what is the laziest thing I could do? For checkout time, the laziest win is skipping verification — auto-filling fields, defaulting to saved data, removing confirmation screens. This is usually done silently in someone's head; it needs to be written down, because the counter-metric only makes sense once the failure mode is explicit.

Step two — pick a counter-metric that would move first, even if the target looks fine. Belani's operations team already had "post-purchase correction rate" — orders edited, cancelled, or disputed within 30 minutes — sitting unused in a different tool. That was the natural counter-metric: it would rise before refund costs or reputational damage showed up, structurally close to the mechanism the target could exploit.

Step three — give the pair one owner, one cadence, one decision. This is the step nearly everyone skips. A counter-metric on someone else's dashboard, reviewed on a different schedule, with no pre-agreed threshold, is decorative. It must sit in the same meeting as the target, owned by whoever has authority to slow the rollout, against a number agreed in advance past which the target is disqualified regardless of how good it looks.

Figure 1. The target metric (checkout time, green) improves smoothly. The counter-metric (correction rate, dashed red) stays flat, then climbs once the team removes verification steps to keep the green line moving — crossing the agreed threshold in week 6, before the town-hall number is announced.

4. The arithmetic Radhika actually ran

Before the town hall, Radhika pulled the numbers herself. Over ten weeks, checkout time fell from 34 to 11 seconds — a 68% reduction, better than the 60% target. Completed-cart rate rose from 71.2% to 76.4%, matching the 1.8%-per-five-seconds relationship the team had modelled; at 210,000 daily sessions that gain was worth roughly ₹5.9 lakh a day, or about ₹4.1 crore over ten weeks — the number the VP wanted in the deck.

The counter-metric told a different story on the same cadence. Post-purchase correction rate had held at 3.1% of orders for eight weeks, then rose to 3.8% in week 8 and 5.6% by week 10 — an 81% relative rise, concentrated exactly when the team shipped the saved-address auto-select and one-tap confirmation skip. At 210,000 orders a day, that 2.5-point rise meant roughly 5,250 additional corrected orders daily. Belani's cost data put an average correction — refund, a 6.5-minute support call at ₹14 a minute, a warehouse re-pick — at about ₹92. So: 5,250 × ₹92 ≈ ₹4.83 lakh a day, or roughly ₹3.4 crore over ten weeks. The programme's net benefit, priced in the target's own currency, was not ₹4.1 crore; it was closer to ₹70 lakh — and shrinking, since correction rate was still climbing.

Second pass — change one input. Suppose the average cost per correction were lower, say ₹55, because most corrections turn out to be simple address edits rather than wrong-item disputes. Then the ten-week cost falls to about ₹2.0 crore and net benefit rises to roughly ₹2.1 crore — still positive, but only once the mix is actually known, which is the follow-up pull Radhika commissioned rather than trust either number alone. The arithmetic does not settle the question; it tells you which one to ask next.
